summary: Defines a YANG data model for the Routing Information Base that aligns with the I2RS RIB information model. It lets network management systems configure and inspect routes in a standard, structured way.

eli5.summary: This is a form with labeled boxes for describing a router's route list, so any management program can fill it in or read it the same way.

subtitle: A standard YANG schema for adding, removing and watching routes and next hops in a router's RIB.

tldr.problem: The Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) needs a machine-readable way for outside clients to read and write a router's Routing Information Base, matching the RIB information model.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8431 defines the YANG module ietf-i2rs-rib: routing instances hold RIBs, RIBs hold routes, routes point to multilevel next hops, and RPCs and notifications let clients change and monitor them.
tldr.outcome: Clients can use NETCONF or RESTCONF to manage RIBs, routes and next hops in a uniform schema, with optional features advertising what each device can do.

facts.label: Next hop preference and weight range

today: RFC 8431 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2018. The metadata for this site shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why a RIB Data Model
sections.content:
The Interface to the Routing System (I2RS, RFC 7921) gives clients read and write access to information and state inside the routing process of routing elements. One of its functions is reading and writing the Routing Information Base (RIB).

The RIB information model is defined in RFC 8430. This document defines a YANG data model (RFC 7950, RFC 6991) that satisfies the RIB use cases and aligns with that information model. Tree diagrams follow the notation of RFC 8340.
sections.eli5: Outside programs need a common language for talking to a router about its routes. This RFC writes down that language.

sections.title: Routing Instances, RIBs and Routes
sections.content:
The top of the module is a routing-instance with a name, an interface list, an optional router-id and an optional lookup-limit. A routing instance is a collection of RIBs, interfaces and routing protocol parameters, and it creates a logical slice of the router. It can hold multiple RIBs, so they are modelled as a list called rib-list, each with a name, an address-family and an optional ip-rpf-check.

A route is essentially a match condition plus an action. The match can be an IPv4, IPv6, MPLS, MAC or interface route, and IP routes can match on destination, source, or both. A route MUST contain the ROUTE_PREFERENCE attribute (lower value means more preferred), and each route is keyed by a route-index.

In responses to RIB reads and writes a route MUST also carry status: Active (at least one fully resolved next hop, so eligible for the FIB), Installed (it got installed in the FIB) and Reason (for a failure, such as "Not authorized").
sections.eli5: Think of a router as a building with several address books. Each entry says: if the destination looks like this, send it that way, and a number says how much to trust the entry.

sections.title: Next Hops
sections.content:
A nexthop is the object resulting from a route lookup. It is modelled as a multilevel structure that supports recursion, so it can express load balancing, protection and multicast. The first level has these types:

  • Base: the foundation of all others, covering a next hop ID, IPv4 or IPv6 address, egress interface (alone or with an IPv4, IPv6 or MAC address), logical tunnel, tunnel encapsulation, tunnel decapsulation and a RIB name.
  • Chain: performs several operations on a packet by combining them.
  • Load-balance: normally several weighted next hops.
  • Protection: normally a primary and a standby next hop.
  • Replicate: forwarding to multiple destinations.

Tunnel encapsulation can describe IPv4, IPv6, MPLS, GRE, NVGRE and VXLAN headers. Protection members carry a preference and load-balance members a weight, both from 1 to 99. A weight of 0 is reserved for equal load balancing and, if used, MUST be applied to all member next hops.
sections.eli5: A next hop is the signpost at the end of a lookup. Some signposts point one way, some split traffic between several ways, and some name a backup road in case the first is closed.

sections.title: RPCs for Changing the RIB
sections.content:
The module defines RPC operations: rib-add, rib-delete, route-add, route-delete, route-update, nh-add and nh-delete. Deleting a RIB deletes all routes installed in it.

Route operations take the RIB name and the routes, plus an indication of whether to return failure details. They return a success-count, a failed-count and, on request, a failure-detail listing the failed routes. route-update can match on route prefixes, route attributes, vendor attributes or next hops, and can update next hops and attributes.

Before calling route-add, a client is required to call nh-add to create the next hop and get its identifier, unless the next hop already exists and its ID is known. The network node allocates the identifier.
sections.eli5: The RPCs are buttons on a remote control: make a list, remove a list, add or change a route, add or remove a signpost. Each button tells you how many things worked and how many did not.

sections.title: Capabilities and Notifications
sections.content:
Not every device supports every kind of next hop or every depth of lookup, so the model uses YANG feature and if-feature statements to advertise capabilities. Features include nexthop-chain, nexthop-protection, nexthop-replicate, nexthop-load-balance, nexthop-tunnel and per-tunnel features such as ipv4-tunnel, mpls-tunnel, vxlan-tunnel and gre-tunnel.

An implementation MUST support two asynchronous notifications. The route-change notification MUST be sent when a route moves between active and inactive, or between installed and uninstalled. The nexthop-resolution-status-change notification reports whether a next hop is resolved or unresolved. An unresolved next hop needs the RIB manager to work out how to reach it, and it is not a suitable candidate for installation in the FIB.

Route change reasons defined in the module include a lower or higher route preference, and a resolved or unresolved next hop.
sections.eli5: Some routers can do fancy tricks and some cannot, so each one shows a list of what it can do. It also rings a bell when a route turns on or off.

sections.title: The YANG Module
sections.content:
Section 3 of the RFC holds the module ietf-i2rs-rib (revision 2018-09-13, prefix iir), the bulk of the document. It imports types from RFC 6991 and interface definitions from RFC 8344, and it defines the features, identities and typedefs described above along with the data tree, RPCs and notifications.

Address families, route types, next hop states, route states and route change reasons are expressed as YANG identities, so other modules can extend them.
sections.eli5: The module is the exact, formal wording of the form, written so computers can check it.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The module is designed to be accessed through NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040). The mandatory-to-implement secure transports are SSH for NETCONF and TLS for RESTCONF. The NETCONF access control model (RFC 8341) restricts users to a subset of operations and content, and the RFC says it should be vigorously applied.

The writable data and RPCs are sensitive. A malicious client could remove or add a RIB, a route or a next hop, which could disrupt service, give suboptimal paths or degrade service levels. Removing a RIB or route could disrupt a service.

IANA registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-i2rs-rib and the YANG module ietf-i2rs-rib with the prefix iir.
sections.eli5: Because the form can change real routes, only trusted people should be allowed to fill it in. A mischievous user could send traffic the wrong way.

viz.caption: RPC OPERATIONS DEFINED BY THE MODULE

items.label: Add a RIB
items.desc: Adds a RIB to a routing instance.

items.label: Delete a RIB
items.desc: Removes the RIB and all its routes.

items.label: Add a next hop
items.desc: Node allocates and returns a next hop identifier.

items.label: Delete a next hop
items.desc: Takes a RIB name and a next hop or its identifier.

items.label: Add routes
items.desc: Adds one or more routes to a RIB.

items.label: Update routes
items.desc: Changes next hops or attributes of matching routes.

items.label: Delete routes
items.desc: Removes one or more routes from a RIB.
